steps.text: This is The Long Map. Book One. The Story of the Jews.
We will follow one people across more than three thousand years. Every line tells you whether it is attested, disputed, or remembered in tradition.
steps.display: We will follow one people across more than 3,000 years. Every line tells you whether it is attested, disputed, or remembered in tradition.

steps.text: The year is about twelve hundred and seven BC. Egypt is still a great empire, and its king is Merneptah, the thirteenth son of Ramesses the Second.
claims: The year is about twelve hundred and seven BC. Egypt is still a great empire, and its king is Merneptah, the thirteenth son of Ramesses the Second.
steps.display: The year is about 1207 BC. Egypt is still a great empire, and its king is Merneptah, the 13th son of Ramesses II.

steps.text: North-east of Egypt, along a desert road of forts called the Ways of Horus, lay Canaan. It was a land of small city-states, each with its own ruler, and Egypt was their overlord.
claims: North-east of Egypt, along a desert road of forts called the Ways of Horus, lay Canaan. It was a land of small city-states, each with its own ruler, and Egypt was their overlord.

steps.text: And in the hills of Canaan lived a people called Israel. We do not know how long they had been there. Most scholars place them in the central hill country.
claims: And in the hills of Canaan lived a people called Israel.
We do not know how long they had been there.
Most scholars place them in the central hill country.

steps.text: Imagine those hills in the evening. Rock and scrub, a few small fields, and smoke rising where a family is cooking.
That is the world of this year. You can stay with the story, or explore the map on your own.
Egypt lived by its river. Each summer the Nile flooded, and left fresh black soil on the fields. From that soil came the wheat and barley that fed the land.
claims: Egypt lived by its river. Each summer the Nile flooded, and left fresh black soil on the fields. From that soil came the wheat and barley that fed the land.

steps.text: Scholars estimate that some three million people lived in Egypt then. Some think it was more. Nobody counted them for us.
claims: Scholars estimate that some three million people lived in Egypt then. Some think it was more. Nobody counted them for us.

steps.text: Egyptian soldiers kept watch at Gaza, on the coast, and at Beth-Shean, in the valley of the Jordan.
claims: Egyptian soldiers kept watch at Gaza, on the coast, and at Beth-Shean, in the valley of the Jordan.

steps.text: The Canaanites had long been at home here. A century earlier, the rulers of Jerusalem, Shechem, Gezer and Megiddo had written clay letters to Pharaoh, each asking for his favour.
claims: The Canaanites had long been at home here. A century earlier, the rulers of Jerusalem, Shechem, Gezer and Megiddo had written clay letters to Pharaoh, each asking for his favour.

steps.text: Their gods were old gods of the land. El was the father of the gods. Baal was the storm god, who brought the rain that the fields depended on.
claims: Their gods were old gods of the land. El was the father of the gods. Baal was the storm god, who brought the rain that the fields depended on.

steps.text: Far to the north, the Hittites ruled from Hattusa, high in Anatolia. Two generations earlier, Egypt and Hatti had fought at Kadesh, and then made one of the oldest peace treaties we know.
claims: Far to the north, the Hittites ruled from Hattusa, high in Anatolia. Two generations earlier, Egypt and Hatti had fought at Kadesh, and then made one of the oldest peace treaties we know.

steps.text: To the east, beyond the Euphrates, Assyria had grown strong. Its king, Tukulti-Ninurta, had plundered Babylon. Around this very time he was killed in a revolt led by his own son.
claims: To the east, beyond the Euphrates, Assyria had grown strong. Its king, Tukulti-Ninurta, had plundered Babylon. Around this very time he was killed in a revolt led by his own son.

steps.text: We know Israel's name because of a stone. In his fifth year, Merneptah set up a victory hymn in his temple at Thebes. It was carved on a slab of grey granite, more than three metres tall.
claims: We know Israel's name because of a stone. In his fifth year, Merneptah set up a victory hymn in his temple at Thebes. It was carved on a slab of grey granite, more than three metres tall.
steps.display: We know Israel's name because of a stone. In his fifth year, Merneptah set up a victory hymn in his temple at Thebes. It was carved on a slab of grey granite, more than 3 metres tall.

steps.text: The stone was not new. His craftsmen carved the hymn on the back of an older stele of Amenhotep the Third. It runs to twenty-eight lines.
claims: The stone was not new. His craftsmen carved the hymn on the back of an older stele of Amenhotep the Third. It runs to twenty-eight lines.
steps.display: The stone was not new. His craftsmen carved the hymn on the back of an older stele of Amenhotep III. It runs to 28 lines.

steps.text: Most of the hymn praises his victory over the Libyans. Only near the very end does it turn to Canaan.
claims: Most of the hymn praises his victory over the Libyans. Only near the very end does it turn to Canaan.

steps.text: Canaan is plundered with every evil. Ashkelon is carried off. Gezer is seized. Yenoam is made non-existent. Israel is laid waste. Its seed is not.

steps.text: Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam are written with the sign for a foreign land. Israel is written with the sign for a people.
claims: Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam are written with the sign for a foreign land. Israel is written with the sign for a people.

steps.text: This is a royal hymn, made to praise the king. Historians debate how much of it describes real battles, and whether seed here means grain, or children.
claims: This is a royal hymn, made to praise the king. Historians debate how much of it describes real battles, and whether seed here means grain, or children.

steps.text: On a wall at Karnak, battle scenes show the taking of Ashkelon. Some scholars think another scene there shows Israel. Others disagree.
claims: On a wall at Karnak, battle scenes show the taking of Ashkelon.
Some scholars think another scene there shows Israel. Others disagree.

steps.text: Either way, Merneptah's stone holds the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible.
claims: Either way, Merneptah's stone holds the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible.

steps.text: In Jewish tradition, the name is older still. The Torah tells how Jacob wrestled through the night, and was told, your name shall be Israel. His descendants became the children of Israel.

steps.text: The Torah tells how they went down to Egypt and were enslaved there, how God brought them out under Moses, and how at Sinai they received the Torah before coming to Canaan.

claims: No Egyptian text found so far names Moses or the Exodus. Scholars differ on how this memory relates to history.

steps.text: For Jews, it is the founding memory, retold every year at Passover. It carries a lesson for every age. Do not wrong the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

transitionOut.text: Next: the hill villages grow over the following generations. In Jewish memory this is the time of the Judges, when the tribes lived without a king.

events.title: A land between empires
events.text: At Kadesh in Syria, Ramesses II of Egypt fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II in one of the largest chariot battles of the ancient world. Both kings claimed victory. Afterwards the frontier settled: the Hittites kept Syria, and Egypt kept Canaan.
events.why: The land where Israel would soon appear lay on Egypt's side of this line. Again and again in Jewish history, life in this narrow land would be shaped by the great powers on either side.
claims: Battle of Kadesh, year 5 of Ramesses II (1274 BC in the usual chronology).
Ramesses' own account of personal triumph is royal propaganda. Most historians see a stalemate.

events.title: Peace between Egypt and Hatti
events.text: In Ramesses II's 21st year, Egypt and the Hittite king Hattusili III made one of the oldest peace treaties known. It was written on silver tablets. Copies survive in hieroglyphs on temple walls at Karnak and the Ramesseum, and in Akkadian on clay tablets found at Hattusa.
events.why: The peace held for the rest of the century. Canaan stayed under Egyptian rule, with its roads, garrisons and tribute. This is the world in which Israel's name first enters writing.
claims: Treaty of year 21 of Ramesses II with Hattusili III.
Egyptian copies at Karnak and the Ramesseum; Akkadian tablets at Hattusa.

events.title: Canaan under Egypt
events.text: Canaan was a patchwork of small city-states, each with its own ruler and Egypt as overlord. Egyptian troops sat at Gaza and Beth-Shean, and a fortified road, the Ways of Horus, linked Egypt to Canaan. A century earlier, local rulers of Jerusalem, Shechem, Gezer and Megiddo wrote clay letters to Pharaoh, each asking for his favour.
events.why: Many of these names run through the Hebrew Bible: Jerusalem, Shechem, Hebron, Megiddo, Hazor, Gezer. They were already old towns long before Israel had kings. The great city of Hazor in the north had probably already been destroyed.
claims: Egyptian garrisons at Gaza and Beth-Shean; forts along the Ways of Horus.
Amarna letters from rulers of Jerusalem, Shechem, Gezer and Megiddo (14th century BC).
Hazor was destroyed in the 13th century BC. Who destroyed it, and exactly when, is disputed.
The Book of Joshua tells that Joshua conquered Hazor and burned it.

events.title: The memory of Egypt
events.text: The Hebrew Bible tells how the children of Israel, descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, went down to Egypt and were enslaved there. God brought them out under the leadership of Moses. At Mount Sinai they received the Torah, and after forty years in the wilderness they came to the land of Canaan.
events.why: For Jews, the Exodus is the founding memory: the story of becoming a free people bound by a covenant with God. It is retold every year at the Passover Seder, and it shapes prayer and law: 'you shall not wrong a stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt' (Exodus 22:21).
claims: The account of slavery, Exodus, Sinai and the wilderness is told in the Torah (Exodus to Deuteronomy).
Exodus 1:11 names the store-cities Pithom and Raamses. Many scholars connect Raamses with Pi-Ramesses, the residence of Ramesses II.
People from Canaan did live and work in New Kingdom Egypt, and Egypt ruled Canaan, so contact between the two lands was real.
No Egyptian text found so far mentions Moses or the Exodus. Scholars differ on how the memory relates to history, from a large historical exodus to the experience of a smaller group.

events.title: Assyria on the rise
events.text: Far to the east, Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeated the Hittites near Nihriya, captured the Babylonian king Kashtiliashu IV and plundered Babylon, carrying off the statue of the god Marduk. He built himself a new capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta. Around 1207 BC he was killed there by one of his sons.
events.why: For now Assyria is far away. Five centuries later Assyria would conquer the kingdom of Israel and take Samaria (722 BC), one of the great turning points in Jewish history.
claims: Reign c. 1243–1207 BC; capture of Kashtiliashu IV and of Babylon.
Killed by his son(s) in a revolt; Ashur-nadin-apli followed.
His claim to have carried off '28,800 Hittites' is a royal boast; the number cannot be checked.

events.title: Famine, war and the 'Sea Peoples'
events.text: In Merneptah's fifth year, Libyans under their chief Meryey invaded Egypt with allies the Egyptians named Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh, groups modern scholars call 'Sea Peoples'. Merneptah defeated them. In the same years he sent grain to the Hittites, as he says, 'to keep alive' the land of Hatti in a famine.
events.why: The old order was starting to break. Over the next decades, palaces fell from Greece to Syria. In the hills of Canaan, a new village society would grow in the gap that opened up, and among the later newcomers on the coast were the Philistines, well known from the Bible.
claims: The Libyan war of year 5 and the named allies come from Merneptah's Great Karnak Inscription.
Grain shipped to Hatti 'to keep alive' the land.
The Bronze Age collapse had many causes, including drought, earthquakes, war and broken trade. How much each mattered is disputed.
The Peleset (Philistines) appear under Ramesses III, a generation later.

events.title: 'Israel' in stone
events.text: In the same year Merneptah set up a victory hymn in his temple at Thebes. Near its end come a few lines about Canaan: 'Canaan is plundered with every evil. Ashkelon is carried off, Gezer is seized, Yenoam is made non-existent. Israel is laid waste, its seed is not.' The cities are written with the sign for a foreign land. Israel is written with the sign for a people.
events.why: This is the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. It shows that a group called Israel lived in Canaan around 1208 BC, distinct enough for Egypt to name it beside the old cities. Pharaoh's boast that Israel was finished did not come true: more than 3,200 years later the name of Israel lives on in the Jewish people.
claims: Text of the Merneptah Stele, year 5. Quotation in standard translation.
Israel is written with the determinative for a people, the cities with the sign for a foreign land.
Whether 'seed' means grain or descendants is debated.
The stele does not say where Israel lived. Most scholars place it in Canaan, many in the central hill country.
Found by Flinders Petrie in 1896 in Merneptah's mortuary temple in western Thebes; the stone is a reused stele of Amenhotep III.

pic.cap: The Merneptah Stele, Egyptian Museum, Cairo. Photograph by Onceinawhile, 2022. CC BY-SA 4.0.

events.title: New villages in the hills
events.text: Over the next two centuries, small farming villages spread across the central hill country, where few people had lived before. Surveys count about 30 sites there in the 13th century BC and about 250 by the end of the Iron Age I, around 1000 BC.
events.why: These hills, around Shechem, Shiloh, Jerusalem and Hebron, became the heartland of the later kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Jewish tradition remembers this as the time of the Judges: 'In those days there was no king in Israel' (Judges 21:25).
claims: About 30 sites and 50 hectares in the 13th century BC; about 250 sites and 220 hectares in late Iron I.
Population about 10,000 rising to about 45,000. These figures are calculated from built-up area, so they are rough.
Many archaeologists identify these villagers with early Israel. Others caution that pottery and houses alone cannot show who people felt they were.
Few or no pig bones are found at these hill sites, and some scholars link this to Israelite identity.
The Book of Judges tells of tribes led by judges such as Deborah and Gideon.

steps.text: In the years after Merneptah's stone, the old world of palaces began to fall. Historians call it the Late Bronze Age collapse.
claims: In the years after Merneptah's stone, the old world of palaces began to fall. Historians call it the Late Bronze Age collapse.

steps.text: It had no single cause. Drought, earthquakes, war and broken trade all played a part, and scholars still argue over which mattered most.
claims: It had no single cause. Drought, earthquakes, war and broken trade all played a part, and scholars still argue over which mattered most.

steps.text: Even before the worst came, there was hunger. Merneptah sent grain by ship to the Hittites, to keep their land alive in a famine.
claims: Even before the worst came, there was hunger. Merneptah sent grain by ship to the Hittites, to keep their land alive in a famine.

steps.text: On the Syrian coast stood Ugarit, a rich trading port. Its scribes wrote in several languages, and in their own alphabet of thirty letters.
claims: On the Syrian coast stood Ugarit, a rich trading port. Its scribes wrote in several languages, and in their own alphabet of thirty letters.
steps.display: On the Syrian coast stood Ugarit, a rich trading port. Its scribes wrote in several languages, and in their own alphabet of 30 letters.

steps.text: By modern estimates, several thousand people lived in the city itself, and many more in its villages.
claims: By modern estimates, several thousand people lived in the city itself, and many more in its villages.

steps.text: A letter from the king of Ugarit to the king of Cyprus survives. My father, behold, the enemy's ships came. My cities were burned, and they did evil things in my country.
claims: A letter from the king of Ugarit to the king of Cyprus survives. My father, behold, the enemy's ships came. My cities were burned, and they did evil things in my country.

steps.text: Around eleven ninety BC, Ugarit was destroyed. It was never rebuilt as a city.
claims: Around eleven ninety BC, Ugarit was destroyed. It was never rebuilt as a city.
steps.display: Around 1190 BC, Ugarit was destroyed. It was never rebuilt as a city.

steps.text: Radiocarbon dates from nearby Tell Tweini point to about eleven ninety-two to eleven ninety BC. Who the attackers were is still debated.
claims: Radiocarbon dates from nearby Tell Tweini point to about eleven ninety-two to eleven ninety BC. Who the attackers were is still debated.
steps.display: Radiocarbon dates from nearby Tell Tweini point to about 1192 to 1190 BC. Who the attackers were is still debated.

steps.text: Far inland, the Hittite court left its capital, Hattusa, and the empire came to an end. Excavators found little sign of a final battle. The court seems to have taken its records and treasures with it.
claims: Far inland, the Hittite court left its capital, Hattusa, and the empire came to an end. Excavators found little sign of a final battle. The court seems to have taken its records and treasures with it.

steps.text: A branch of the royal family held on at Carchemish, beside the Euphrates.
claims: A branch of the royal family held on at Carchemish, beside the Euphrates.

steps.text: In Egypt, Ramesses the Third had these words carved at Medinet Habu. The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. No land could stand before their arms.
claims: In Egypt, Ramesses the Third had these words carved at Medinet Habu. The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. No land could stand before their arms.
steps.display: In Egypt, Ramesses III had these words carved at Medinet Habu. The foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands. No land could stand before their arms.

steps.text: The same temple walls show people on the move by land, with ox-carts carrying women and children.
claims: The same temple walls show people on the move by land, with ox-carts carrying women and children.

steps.text: Modern historians call them the Sea Peoples. Where they came from, how many they were, and how much they caused the collapse, are all debated. Many were probably looking for a new home.
claims: Modern historians call them the Sea Peoples. Where they came from, how many they were, and how much they caused the collapse, are all debated. Many were probably looking for a new home.

steps.text: In his eighth year, around eleven seventy-seven BC, Ramesses the Third met them on land, in a region the Egyptians called Djahy.
claims: In his eighth year, around eleven seventy-seven BC, Ramesses the Third met them on land, in a region the Egyptians called Djahy.
steps.display: In his eighth year, around 1177 BC, Ramesses III met them on land, in a region the Egyptians called Djahy.

steps.text: Where exactly Djahy lay, and where the battle was fought, is debated.

steps.label: Sea battle at the Nile mouths

steps.text: Then he fought them at sea, at the mouths of the Nile. His temple walls show ships locked together, and Egyptian archers shooting from the shore.
claims: Then he fought them at sea, at the mouths of the Nile. His temple walls show ships locked together, and Egyptian archers shooting from the shore.

steps.text: Ramesses claimed a great victory, and Egypt itself was not overrun.
claims: Ramesses claimed a great victory, and Egypt itself was not overrun.

steps.text: Among the enemies, the inscriptions name the Peleset. We know them better as the Philistines.
claims: Among the enemies, the inscriptions name the Peleset. We know them better as the Philistines.

steps.text: A later papyrus says Ramesses settled the defeated in strongholds. Whether that means Egypt itself placed the Philistines in Canaan is debated.
claims: A later papyrus says Ramesses settled the defeated in strongholds.
Whether that means Egypt itself placed the Philistines in Canaan is debated.

steps.text: On the southern coast of Canaan, newcomers made four towns their own. Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Gath.
claims: On the southern coast of Canaan, newcomers made four towns their own. Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Gath.

steps.text: They brought their own ways. Their painted pottery followed Aegean styles. They cooked on open hearths, and wove with loom weights shaped like spools.
claims: They brought their own ways. Their painted pottery followed Aegean styles. They cooked on open hearths, and wove with loom weights shaped like spools.

steps.text: They also ate a good deal of pork, unlike the villagers in the hills.
claims: They also ate a good deal of pork, unlike the villagers in the hills.

steps.text: Ancient DNA from Ashkelon shows that some of the early settlers had ancestry from southern Europe. Within about two centuries, their families had mixed with the people of the land.
claims: Ancient DNA from Ashkelon shows that some of the early settlers had ancestry from southern Europe. Within about two centuries, their families had mixed with the people of the land.

steps.text: When they arrived is debated. The usual view says about eleven seventy-five BC. A lower dating says about eleven thirty-five.
claims: When they arrived is debated. The usual view says about eleven seventy-five BC. A lower dating says about eleven thirty-five.
steps.display: When they arrived is debated. The usual view says about 1175 BC. A lower dating says about 1135 BC.

steps.text: The Hebrew Bible remembers the Philistines as coming from Caphtor, and as Israel's great rivals in the days of the Judges, of Samson, and of Saul.
claims: The Hebrew Bible remembers the Philistines as coming from Caphtor, and as Israel's great rivals in the days of the Judges, of Samson, and of Saul.

steps.text: Imagine the coast in those years. New houses going up, unfamiliar words in the market, and families learning a new land, as so many families have done since.
Egypt held on in Canaan for some decades more, with soldiers still at Beth-Shean. But during the twelfth century its rule there came to an end.
claims: Egypt held on in Canaan for some decades more, with soldiers still at Beth-Shean. But during the twelfth century its rule there came to an end.
steps.display: Egypt held on in Canaan for some decades more, with soldiers still at Beth-Shean. But during the 12th century BC its rule there came to an end.

steps.text: Whether the end came quickly, or slowly over seventy-five years or more, is still debated.
claims: Whether the end came quickly, or slowly over seventy-five years or more, is still debated.
steps.display: Whether the end came quickly, or slowly over 75 years or more, is still debated.

steps.text: And in the hills, something new was growing. Small farming villages spread across the central hill country, where few people had lived before.
claims: And in the hills, something new was growing. Small farming villages spread across the central hill country, where few people had lived before.

steps.text: Surveys count about thirty sites there in the thirteenth century BC, and about two hundred and fifty by around one thousand BC.
claims: Surveys count about thirty sites there in the thirteenth century BC, and about two hundred and fifty by around one thousand BC.
steps.display: Surveys count about 30 sites there in the 13th century BC, and about 250 by around 1000 BC.

steps.text: Many archaeologists see these villagers as early Israel. Others caution that houses and pottery alone cannot tell us what people called themselves.

steps.text: Where they came from is debated too. Some scholars think they were herders of the region, settling down. Others think many came from the Canaanite towns of the lowlands.
claims: Where they came from is debated too. Some scholars think they were herders of the region, settling down. Others think many came from the Canaanite towns of the lowlands.

steps.text: Imagine the hills at dawn. Rock and scrub, smoke from cooking fires, and flocks heading out to graze. Here is what the excavations show.
Most villages were small, often a few dozen households. Some of the earliest, like Izbet Sartah, were a ring of houses around an open yard.
claims: Most villages were small, often a few dozen households. Some of the earliest, like Izbet Sartah, were a ring of houses around an open yard.

steps.text: A typical home was a pillared house, with three or four spaces around a central room.
claims: A typical home was a pillared house, with three or four spaces around a central room.

steps.text: Animals and stores were probably kept on the ground floor, with the family living above. Not every scholar agrees.
claims: Animals and stores were probably kept on the ground floor, with the family living above. Not every scholar agrees.

steps.text: Families stored grain in pits lined with stone, and in large jars with a collar around the neck. They cut cisterns into the rock, to keep the winter rain for the dry summer.
claims: Families stored grain in pits lined with stone, and in large jars with a collar around the neck. They cut cisterns into the rock, to keep the winter rain for the dry summer.

steps.text: On steeper slopes, terraces held the soil. How early these terraces were built is debated.
claims: On steeper slopes, terraces held the soil.
How early these terraces were built is debated.

steps.text: They grew wheat and barley, tended olives and vines, and herded sheep and goats.
claims: They grew wheat and barley, tended olives and vines, and herded sheep and goats.

steps.text: Bread was the staple food. Grinding stones for flour are common finds in these houses, and grinding was hard daily work.
claims: Bread was the staple food. Grinding stones for flour are common finds in these houses, and grinding was hard daily work.

steps.text: Scholars think it was mostly women who did it, for hours each day.
claims: Scholars think it was mostly women who did it, for hours each day.

steps.text: The Torah would later praise this land as a land of wheat and barley, of vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey.
claims: The Torah would later praise this land as a land of wheat and barley, of vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey.

steps.text: Pig bones are rare at these hill sites. Some scholars link this to the later Jewish law against eating pork. Others think it was simply how hill farmers lived.
claims: Pig bones are rare at these hill sites.
Some scholars link this to the later Jewish law against eating pork. Others think it was simply how hill farmers lived.

steps.text: At Izbet Sartah, someone scratched an alphabet onto a piece of pottery, perhaps while learning to write. How old it is exactly is debated.
claims: At Izbet Sartah, someone scratched an alphabet onto a piece of pottery, perhaps while learning to write.
How old it is exactly is debated.

steps.text: On a hilltop in the north of these hills, archaeologists found a small open-air shrine, and a bronze figure of a bull. Who worshipped there, and which god, is debated.
claims: On a hilltop in the north of these hills, archaeologists found a small open-air shrine, and a bronze figure of a bull.
Who worshipped there, and which god, is debated.

steps.text: The name Israel itself contains El, the old word for God across Canaan.
claims: The name Israel itself contains El, the old word for God across Canaan.

steps.text: An Egyptian list from more than a century earlier names a land of the Shasu, Yhw. Some read this as the name of Israel's God. Others doubt it.

steps.text: Down on the coast and along the trade roads, the long-distance trade in copper, tin and fine goods that had fed the palaces had faltered.
claims: Down on the coast and along the trade roads, the long-distance trade in copper, tin and fine goods that had fed the palaces had faltered.

steps.text: For Israel, the world nearby had changed. The empire that named it in stone was withdrawing. The Philistines were new neighbours on the coast. And the hill villages kept growing.
claims: For Israel, the world nearby had changed. The empire that named it in stone was withdrawing. The Philistines were new neighbours on the coast. And the hill villages kept growing.

steps.text: Imagine a winter evening in one of these houses. Rain on the roof, the animals shifting nearby. We do not know these villagers' names. Their houses, jars and terraces are what they left us.

steps.text: Many scholars count the Song of Deborah, in the Book of Judges, among the oldest poems in the Hebrew Bible. It names tribes who came to fight, and some who stayed at home.

steps.text: There is no kingdom yet. For now, this is a people of villages, in a land shared with others. Their story has only begun.
